title: Foam in the line
note: Fictional patients and staff. Your unit’s emergency protocol and the physician come first.
intro:
You are the charge nurse. It is Thursday, 14:32. Mr. Benito Santos, 63, at Bed 12, has a central venous catheter and is 50 minutes into treatment. He suddenly coughs, grabs his chest, and slumps. The machine’s air detector is alarming, and there is foam in the venous line. He is not responding and not breathing normally.

Eleven other patients are connected. Your nurses on the floor are Arnel, Kris, and Mika. The physician on duty is about five minutes away.

n1.prompt: Is the circuit the cause or a bystander, and what happens to it?

choices.text: The cause: keep the pump stopped, clamp, do not return the blood, and resuscitate.
choices.feedback: Air or foam in the venous line means the circuit may be the cause. Blood that may contain air is never returned. When in doubt, stop, clamp, and resuscitate.

choices.text: A bystander: return the blood quickly so he has the volume for resuscitation, then disconnect him and move him to the floor.
choices.feedback: Returning blood through a line with air in it can push more air into him. The return-the-blood rule applies only when the circuit is a bystander: no air, no blood loss, normal line color, no pattern in other chairs.
choices.then: Arnel stops you before the saline runs. The lines are clamped.

choices.text: Clear the air alarm and look along the line for where the air got in.
choices.feedback: The source can be found later. He has no pulse. Clamp, leave the blood in the circuit, and start resuscitation.
choices.then: You clamp the lines and call the code.

choices.text: “Bed 12, no pulse. Arnel, compressions. Kris, defibrillator. Mika, watch everyone else. I’ll lead.”
choices.feedback: Named roles, said aloud. The watcher is the role most often forgotten and the one most specific to dialysis: eleven other patients are still connected.

choices.text: “Code at Bed 12! Someone get the cart!” and start compressions yourself.
choices.feedback: Unnamed requests are the ones nobody does. And with you at the chest, nobody is leading and nobody is watching the other patients.
choices.then: You hand compressions to Arnel and give named roles.

choices.text: “Arnel, compressions. Kris, defibrillator and airway bag. Mika, help Kris with the pads and the monitor.”
choices.feedback: Good named tasks, but no one is watching the eleven other patients, some losing pressure, some with needles that can come out while everyone looks at Bed 12.

n3.scene: Kris went for the defibrillator 90 seconds ago. You have heard nothing back.

choices.text: “Kris, pads on?” and wait for “Pads on.”
choices.feedback: Name, task, repeat back, report done. A closed loop tells you the task happened. In emergency simulations, requests with a named recipient and a closed loop were completed every time.
choices.then: “Pads on.” The rhythm is not shockable. Compressions continue.

choices.text: Assume it is done and carry on.
choices.feedback: Silence is not a report. In an arrest, an assumed task is the one that turns out not to have happened.
choices.then: At the next check you ask. Kris is still searching for pads. They go on a minute later. The rhythm is not shockable.

choices.text: Go and get the pads yourself, since you know exactly where they are kept and it will be quicker than asking.
choices.feedback: The pads arrive, but the code has no leader while you are away. Ask for the report instead.
choices.then: Pads go on. The rhythm is not shockable.

choices.text: Stay. “Kris, Bed 5: stop fluid removal, lay him flat, recheck in two minutes, report to me.”
choices.feedback: When two things happen at once, the charge nurse keeps the sicker patient and sends her most experienced available nurse to the other, with a named task and a report-back time.

choices.text: Leave the code to Arnel, who is doing compressions well, and go to Bed 5 yourself because you are the most experienced.
choices.feedback: The patient in arrest is the sicker one. Leaving the code without a leader risks both patients. Delegate Bed 5 with a named task.
choices.then: You return to Bed 12 and send Kris to Bed 5 with a task and a report time.

choices.feedback: Mika is the watcher; if she goes, nobody watches the other ten. And “sort it out” is not a task. Send another nurse with specific steps and a report time.
choices.then: You redirect: Kris to Bed 5 with steps; Mika keeps watching.

choices.text: Who, collapse time, air in the line, time on dialysis, fluid removed, last potassium, blood not returned, CPR and rhythm.
choices.feedback: Who, what happened and when, what was done, the dialysis details, and what is pending. The receiving team cannot guess the time on the machine, the fluid removed, the last potassium, the access, or whether blood was returned and why.

choices.text: “Bed 12, Mr. Santos, arrested about five minutes ago on dialysis; we started CPR straight away and the pads are on.”
choices.feedback: True, but the physician must now ask for everything else. Give the time, the suspected air, the dialysis details, and what has been done.

choices.text: Let the physician read the treatment sheet while you go back to the floor.
choices.feedback: The sheet does not say what happened in the last five minutes. A structured handoff takes under a minute and prevents repeated or missed steps.

end.title: After the code
end.text: The physician leads the resuscitation and the transfer. You keep the lines and the catheter connections for inspection, take the machine out of use for the biomedical team, and hold a short team debrief the same day. The incident report gives the facts and times without blame, and the review asks how air entered the circuit.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Cause or bystander? Air, blood loss, dark or translucent blood, wrong dialysate, or a pattern in other chairs: the circuit may be the cause. Stop, clamp, do not return the blood.
  • Roles out loud, by name, including a watcher for every other patient.
  • Close the loop: name, task, repeat back, report done.
  • Two emergencies: keep the sicker patient, send your most experienced nurse with a named task and a report-back time.
  • Hand off the dialysis details the receiving team cannot guess.

See Cause or bystander, Roles out loud and The handoff.
